analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for corporate anti-union campaigns and requires public reporting of that spending.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 139 cosponsors and died in committee without a vote or hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny employers a federal tax deduction for money spent trying to influence their workers' decisions about unions — anti-union meetings, consultants, and related legal costs — and require employers to report that spending to the IRS with penalties for failure to do so. Today, an employer that spends millions opposing a union drive deducts that spending as an ordinary business cost, so other taxpayers effectively help pay for it. The bill treats it like political campaign spending, which the tax code already does not allow as a deduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union, because the money employers spend to oppose organizing would no longer be subsidized by other taxpayers, and because employers would have to disclose what they spend on it. Unions would also benefit from a less subsidized opposition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies a tax deduction for employer spending aimed at influencing employees about labor organizations, ending a public subsidy for anti-union campaigns.
Employers would have to report the dates, amounts, and nature of union-influence activities to the IRS, with penalties of at least $10,000 — or $1,000 per full-time employee — for failing to report.
Third-party consultants hired to run anti-union campaigns would have to file their own reports identifying the employer they worked for.

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 in 10 union elections in 2016-2017, and that companies spend about $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions.

The bill explicitly preserves deductions for ordinary collective bargaining, grievance procedures, labor-management partnerships, communications required by law, and voluntary union recognition, so routine labor relations are not penalized.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run anti-union campaigns would pay more taxes, since spending that was previously deductible would no longer be. Businesses with heavy union-related litigation or consulting costs would bear the largest burden.

drawbacks.text: Covered costs would be broad: the bill treats wages and administrative costs of any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed as non-deductible, which would sweep in many ordinary workplace communications and could be hard for large employers to track.

Employers could face deductions denied based on NLRB complaints or settlements before any final finding against them, effectively penalizing spending on allegations that are later resolved in the employer's favor.
Opponents would argue this selectively raises the cost of employer speech in workplace disputes, an area where employers maintain they have a lawful right to communicate their views to employees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — no tax subsidy for anti-union campaigns — is straightforward and mirrors existing treatment of political lobbying and campaign spending. The serious design concern is overbreadth: denying deductions for wages and costs of any meeting where unions are discussed, and tying deduction loss to mere NLRB complaints or settlements, would hit routine workplace communications and unproven allegations, not just genuine union-busting. The disclosure provisions are less controversial but add compliance burdens. A narrower draft could achieve the main goal with fewer side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2023, by Rep. Donald Norcross with 138 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote.
No further action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that spend heavily on anti-union campaigns keep their tax deduction, since the bill died without a vote. Union-avoidance consultants keep a client market that is cheaper for their clients because of the tax treatment.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 138 of 139 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican (Rep. Fitzpatrick) joining; no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and labor relations law firms
industries.note: Consultants who run employer anti-union campaigns would lose the tax-deductible status of their clients' spending and would face new reporting requirements. The bill's findings cite about $340 million a year spent on such consultants.

Employers would pay the full, unsubsidized cost of anti-union campaigns and would face penalties of at least $10,000 (or $1,000 per employee) for failing to report union-influence spending. Their interest in keeping deductions runs against workers' interest in uncoerced union decisions.

Union organizing drives would face less employer-funded opposition, since the tax subsidy for that opposition would end and spending would be disclosed. Unions themselves are explicitly exempt from the deduction denial.
